content: The prevalence of the Ala581Gly mutation in Eastern and Southern Africa is less than 5%, while the Lys540Glu mutation is present in 60% or more of cases. Resistance levels are categorized as low (Ala581Gly <5%), high (Lys540Glu ≥60% and Ala581Gly <5%), and very high (Lys540Glu ≥60% and Ala581Gly ≥5%). The certainty of evidence for these outcomes ranges from very low to moderate. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) considered several outcomes important, with moderate-certainty evidence supporting their conclusions. The GDG observed that intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (IPTp-SP) has a sustained impact across all transmission and resistance settings. Consequently, the overall certainty of evidence for the outcomes of interest was deemed moderate, reflecting the contribution of numerous observational studies alongside robust data from randomized controlled trials. Further details on evidence certainty assessments are available in the research evidence section online or in the annex of the PDF version. The preferences and values of the target population were determined through consultations with civil society, which highlighted the prioritization of malaria chemoprevention for pregnant women in endemic areas. Contextual factors from studies on IPTp-SP were synthesized, although data on how the intervention was valued were limited. The GDG vote on values and preferences was split between probably no important uncertainty or variability and possibly important uncertainty or variability in how IPTp outcomes are valued across contexts. The consensus was not to assert variability in values but to acknowledge the two positions. More information can be found in the civil society consultation report. The GDG considered IPTp-SP to be cost-effective compared to no intervention, with negligible costs and savings associated with its implementation. Socioeconomic factors such as age, marital status, education, employment, and wealth index influenced the uptake of IPTp-SP. Younger women under 20 years were less likely to receive three doses, while those aged 25–34 were most likely. Higher uptake was associated with being married, having higher education, and being employed. Women in the middle to richest wealth categories had higher uptake compared to those in the poorest categories. Rural residence was inconsistently associated with improved uptake, with some studies reporting higher uptake in rural areas and others in urban settings. Living more than 5 km from a health facility was linked to poorer uptake. Addressing inequities in IPTp programs is likely to improve coverage and pregnancy outcomes. The GDG concluded that IPTp-SP is feasible to implement as it is delivered through antenatal care (ANC) services. However, barriers such as limited staff training, stockouts of SP, under-prescription, and inadequate staffing were noted. Directly observed therapy (DOT) was generally associated with improved uptake, though its utilization varied widely. Despite high SP resistance, IPTp-SP continues to yield positive outcomes for maternal and fetal health, possibly through non-malarial pathways such as reduced bacterial infections or inflammation. Perennial malaria chemoprevention (PMC), formerly known as intermittent preventive treatment in infants (IPTi), involves administering antimalarial medicines at predefined intervals to prevent illness in children in moderate to high perennial malaria transmission settings. The intervention aims to protect young children by maintaining preventive drug concentrations in the blood. The updated recommendation extends PMC to children aged 12–24 months, reflecting evidence of its sustained impact beyond infancy. The GDG determined that PMC is cost-effective, particularly when delivered through the Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) platform using inexpensive drugs like SP. However, cost-effectiveness decreases in low-burden settings or with more expensive medicines. The GDG highlighted the need for routine monitoring of PMC programs to assess safety and impact. Drug resistance remains a concern, as the duration of SP protection is reduced in settings with high resistance. While SP has shown efficacy in reducing clinical malaria, its protective effect diminishes in areas with high resistance mutations. The GDG emphasized the importance of considering contextual factors, such as values and preferences of end-users, costs, and sustainability, when implementing PMC. Co-administration of PMC with other interventions, such as the RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine, requires further research. The GDG used the GRADE framework to develop these recommendations, informed by systematic reviews and evidence from trials and observational studies. The main outcomes of interest included maternal anemia, low birth weight, clinical malaria, and adverse pregnancy outcomes. The GDG concluded that IPTp-SP and PMC are effective interventions for reducing malaria burden and improving health outcomes in endemic areas.
